'''Carolina Algonquian''' (also known as '''''Pamlico''''', ''Croatoan'') is an extinct [[Algonquian languages|Algonquian language]] of the Eastern Algonquian subgroup formerly spoken in North Carolina, United States.<ref>Raymond G. Gordon Jr., ed.  2005.  ''Ethnologue:  Languages of the World''.  15th edition.  Dallas:  Summer Institute of Linguistics.</ref> 

==Classification==
[[File:North carolina algonkin-rituale02.jpg|right|200px|thumb|Watercolor by [[John White (colonist and artist)|John White]] of [[Roanoke (tribe)|Roanoke]] Indians]]
Carolina Algonquian forms a part of the same language group as [[Powhatan language|Powhatan]] or ''Virginia Algonquian'', a  similarly [[extinct language]] of the Eastern Algonquian subgroup of the Algonquian language family, itself a member of the Algic language family.

==History==
[[File:ThomasHarriot.jpg|thumb|right|150px|[[Thomas Harriot]] translated and learned the Carolina Algonquian language from Wanchese and Manteo.]]
In 1584 [[Sir Walter Raleigh]] had dispatched the first of a number of expeditions to [[Roanoke Island]] to explore and eventually settle the New World. Early encounters with the natives were friendly, and, despite the difficulties in communication, the explorers were able to persuade "two of the savages, being {{Not a typo|lustie}} men, whose names were [[Wanchese (chief)|Wanchese]] and [[Manteo (Croatan)|Manteo]]" to accompany them on the return voyage to London,<ref>Milton, p.63</ref> in order for the English people to report both the conditions of the [[New World]] that they had explored and what the usefulness of the territory might be to the English.<ref>Mancall, Peter C.  ''Hakluyt's Promise: An Elizabethan's Obsession for an English America''.  New Haven: Yale University Press, 2007.  159.</ref><ref>Vaughan, Alden T. "Sir Walter Raleigh's Indian Interpreters, 1584-1618."  The William and Mary Quarterly  59.2 (2002): 346-347.</ref>

Once safely delivered to England, the two Indians quickly made a sensation at court. Raleigh's priority, however, was not publicity but rather intelligence about his new land of Virginia. He restricted access to the exotic newcomers, assigning the scientist [[Thomas Harriot]] the job of deciphering and learning the Carolina Algonquian language,<ref>Milton, p.70</ref> using a [[Phonetic transcription|phonetic alphabet]] of his own invention in order to effect the translation.
